Effective spin-1 breathing kagome Hamiltonian induced by the exchange hierarchy in the maple leaf mineral bluebellite

Pratyay Ghosh Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ct.qmat, Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland Campus Süd, Würzburg 97074, Germany    Tobias Müller Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ct.qmat, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland Campus Süd, Würzburg 97074, Germany    Yasir Iqbal Affiliation: Department of Physics and Quantum Centers in Diamond and Emerging Materials (QuCenDiEM) group, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India    Ronny Thomale Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ct.qmat, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland Campus Süd, Würzburg 97074, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics and Quantum Centers in Diamond and Emerging Materials (QuCenDiEM) group, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India    Harald O. Jeschke Affiliation: Research Institute for Interdisciplinary Science, Okayama University, Okayama 700-8530, Japan Affiliation: Department of Physics and Quantum Centers in Diamond and Emerging Materials (QuCenDiEM) group, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India
Abstract

As a highly frustrated model Hamiltonian with an exact dimer ground state, the Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the maple leaf lattice is of high theoretical interest, and a material realization is intensely sought after. We determine the magnetic Hamiltonian of the copper mineral bluebellite using density functional theory based energy mapping. As a consequence of the significant distortion of the spin S=1/2S=1/2 maple leaf lattice, we find two of the five distinct nearest neighbor couplings to be ferromagnetic. Solution of this Hamiltonian with density matrix renormalization group calculations points us to the surprising insight that this particular imperfect maple leaf lattice, due to the strongly ferromagnetic Cu2+ dimer, realizes an effective S=1S=1 breathing kagome Hamiltonian. In fact, this is another highly interesting Hamiltonian which has rarely been realized in materials. Analysis of the effective model within a bond-operator formalism allows us to identify a valence bond solid ground state and to extract thermodynamic quantities using a low-energy bosonic mean-field theory. We resolve the puzzle of the apparent one-dimensional character of bluebellite as our calculated specific heat has a Bonner-Fisher-like shape, in good agreement with experiment.

Triangular motifs in quantum antiferromagnets are a source of geometric frustration and lead to highly nontrivial emergent phenomena like quantum spin liquids [1]. Starting with the triangular lattice, site depletion leads to new lattices which have lower coordination number but potentially more frustration [2, 3]. For example, the kagome lattice is obtained by a 1/41/4 site-depletion of the triangular lattice and has coordination number of four; it also hosts some of the most intensively studied spin liquid candidates [4]. In a somewhat more exotic manner, the maple leaf lattice can be viewed as a one-seventh site-depleted triangular lattice and has a coordination number of five [5]. The uniform nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnetic model on this lattice has been solved via exact diagonalization and other techniques [6, 7] and found a magnetically ordered ground state. Recently, in an analytic work on the model with a bond anisotropy, Ghosh et. al. established an exact dimer ground state [8], making the maple leaf lattice the only other two-dimensional lattice with uniform tiling that admits an exact dimer ground state besides the widely known Shastry-Sutherland model [9] which has an extremely rich phenomenology and phase diagram [10, 11, 12, 13]. While SrCu2​(BO3​)2\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{BO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}} has been found to be an extremely good representation of the Shastry-Sutherland Hamiltonian, a material realizing the model proposed by Ghosh et. al. on the maple leaf lattice has yet to be identified. Candidates involving quantum spins are the copper minerals [14, 15] spangolite Cu6​Al(SO4​)(OH)12​Cl⋅3​H2​O\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{Al}\text{(}\text{SO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}\text{)}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{12}}\text{}}\text{Cl}\,{\cdot}\,\text{3}\,\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O} [16], sabelliite Cu2​ZnAsO4​(OH)3\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{ZnAsO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} [17], mojaveite Cu6​TeO4​(OH)9​Cl\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{TeO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{9}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{9}}\text{}}\text{Cl} [1], fuetterite Pb3​Cu6​TeO6​(OH)7​Cl5\text{Pb}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{TeO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{7}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{7}}\text{}}\text{Cl}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} [19] and finally bluebellite Cu6​IO3​(OH)10​Cl\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{10}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{10}}\text{}}\text{Cl} [1]. Magnetic properties have been characterized experimentally for spangolite [20] and bluebellite [2], but the magnetic Hamiltonians for any of these maple leaf compounds remains to be established.

Here, we focus on bluebellite and resolve the most pressing issues for this prime example of a maple leaf antiferromagnet: we determine all relevant exchange interactions and solve the resulting Hamiltonian employing numerical and semi-analytical techniques. In particular, we address the question raised by experiment: why do the susceptibility and specific heat of bluebellite appear to have a Bonner-Fisher type shape, suggestive of one-dimensional systems? An answer to this question based on order-by-disorder was attempted without knowledge of the Hamiltonian [22]. Methodologically, we apply the energy mapping technique which has proved valuable in extracting the Hamiltonian couplings for many important quantum spin systems [23, 24, 25, 26]. By virtue of a statistical approach and by extracting more than the apparently important exchange interactions, this method has led to surprising insights and met with much success for many materials [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. We then perform density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations [34] on the resulting maple leaf Hamiltonian. This method has been instrumental in furthering the comprehension of the physics of the kagome lattice antiferromagnet [35, 36]. Our DMRG calculations show that bluebellite has a gapped valence bond solid ground state. In order to deepen our understanding, we develop a low-energy theory by implementing the standard bond operator formalism [3]. This theory permits one to perform calculations directly in the thermodynamic limit, obtain static and dynamical structure factors, and assess the behavior of thermodynamic quantities. The analytical and numerical calculations reveal that the bluebellite magnetic interactions very closely emulate an effective S=1S=1 kagome Hamiltonian with a strong breathing anisotropy. So far, the possible S=1S=1 kagome candidates, e.g., KV3​Ge2​O9\text{KV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{Ge}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{9}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{9}}\text{}} [38], NaV6​O11\text{NaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{11}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{11}}\text{}} [39], m​–​MPYNN⋅BF4\mathrm{m\mbox{--}MPYNN\cdot BF_{4}} [40], all undergo lattice distortions at low temperatures. By establishing the connection between maple leaf and kagome, our work paves the pathway to possible realizations and synthesis of new effective S=1S=1 kagome compounds emerging out of S=1/2S=1/2 maple-leaf systems. As an experimental outlook, this enables the study of integer-spin highly frustrated kagome antiferromagnets, notably magnetization plateaus, excitations, and topological properties.

Model Hamiltonian.- Before we could extract the parameters of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian H=∑i<jJi​j​𝐒^i⋅𝐒^jH=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j} for bluebellite, we had to perform a relaxation of the internal positions of H, O and Cl while keeping Cu and I positions, as well as the lattice parameters fixed; this is necessary to sort out some obvious distortions in the experimentally determined room temperature structure [2, 41]. Note, that the maple leaf lattice in the structure of synthetic bluebellite is much more regular compared to the structure of the mineral [1]. In applying the energy mapping technique, we make no assumptions as to which are the important exchange paths. Rather, we determine 20 couplings up to a Cu-Cu distance of 5.9 Å which is about twice the nearest neighbor distance. In Fig. 1 (a), we show how the first eight Heisenberg Hamiltonian parameters evolve with on-site Coulomb interaction UU applied to the strongly correlated Cu2+ 3​d3d orbitals. The relevant UU value is determined by calculating the Curie-Weiss temperature as θCW=−13S(S+1)∑iziJi\theta_{\rm CW}=-\frac{1}{3}S(S+1)\sum_{i}z_{i}J_{i} where ziz_{i} are the coordination numbers of JiJ_{i} and demanding that it matches the experimentally observed value θCW=−34.7\theta_{\rm CW}=-34.7 K [2]. The result for the five maple leaf couplings is J1=−120.8​(1.3)J_{1}=-120.8(1.3) K, J2=88.6​(1.2)J_{2}=88.6(1.2) K, J3=−93.7​(1.0)J_{3}=-93.7(1.0) K, J4=147.6​(1.3)J_{4}=147.6(1.3) K, J5=61.3​(7)J_{5}=61.3(7) K. At first glance, it is disappointing that two of the five couplings are ferromagnetic, making this Hamiltonian very distant from the ideal maple leaf antiferromagnet [8]. But the mixed ferro- and antiferromagnetic (FM and AFM) bluebellite Hamiltonian may attain very attractive properties. First of all, the strongest AFM J4J_{4} would try to enforce a 120∘120^{\circ} order on the J4J_{4} triangles. However, it might not be sufficient to establish a full magnetic order on the system, as the J5J_{5} bonds, which forms the other set of triangles on the lattice, is the weakest. On the other hand, the second strongest AFM J2J_{2} bonds form hexagons of alternating interactions with the FM J3J_{3} bonds, which might promote a dimerized singlet state on the hexagons. Finally, the strong FM J1J_{1} bond might try to project an effective spin-11 on them and reduce the quantum fluctuations of the system. The complex interplay of all these effects makes the properties of bluebellite extremely intricate and intriguing, which we attempt to understand in the rest of this communication.

Ground State.- First, we study the ground state of bluebellite with DMRG by using the iTENSOR library [5]. On three distinct lattice sizes—4848, 108108, and 192192 site clusters—we conduct 2424–3030 sweeps while maintaining a maximum bond dimension of 20482048 [41]. Based on finite-size-scaling, we reveal a magnetically disordered ground state with an energy per site E0/J~=−0.217​(1)E_{0}/\widetilde{J}=-0.217(1), which is gapped by Δ/J~=0.106​(2)\Delta/\widetilde{J}=0.106(2) (J~=J12+J22+J32+J42+J52=238​ K\widetilde{J}=\sqrt{J_{1}^{2}+J_{2}^{2}+J_{3}^{2}+J_{4}^{2}+J_{5}^{2}}=238\text{ K} set as the energy scale) [41]. We show the spin-spin correlations, ⟨S→i⋅S→j⟩\langle\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}\rangle, for all nearest-neighbor spin pairs, S→i\vec{S}_{i} and S→j\vec{S}_{j}, in Fig. 1 (d), which shows strong singlet formation in the spin pairs across the AFM J2J_{2} bonds. This dimerization propensity on the J2J_{2} bonds is indicative of a valence bond solid (VBS) state.

For such a dimerized system, further critical insights can be obtained from the bond operator formalism [3], which provides a suitable way to construct an effective low-energy bosonic theory in the thermodynamic limit. In bond operator representation, one transforms the spin basis to a dimer basis by writing the singlet and three triplet states on a bond as bosons (deemed as bond operators). In our analysis, the J2J_{2} bonds define the dimers. We assume a singlet background (a product state of singlets on the J2J_{2} bonds) as a mean-field, and the triplon (dispersing triplet) excitations on the singlet are treated systematically while ignoring any triplon-triplon interaction (details in the Supplemental Material [41] which contains additional Refs. [6, 7, 8]). This method has been successful in describing the ground state as well as thermodynamic properties of several magnetic materials [4, 47, 48, 49, 50]. The results from this bosonic theory agree well with the DMRG calculations. It finds a stable VBS ground state with energy E0/J~=−0.22494E_{0}/\widetilde{J}=-0.22494 and a spin gap of Δ/J~=0.13474\Delta/\widetilde{J}=0.13474. The spin-spin correlations on all the bonds also agree with the DMRG results; the strongest, on the J2J_{2} bonds, for example, is found to be −0.57570-0.57570 (compare with Fig. 1 (e)).

Apart from the strong singlets forming on the AFM J2J_{2} bonds, the spins connected by FM J1J_{1} interactions develop strong ferromagnetic correlations. The total spin moment on these FM bonds is estimated to be approximately 1.81.8 from both methods, signalling the system’s tendency to satisfy the strongest FM bond J1J_{1} by forming triplets so that the S=1/2S=1/2 astride the J1J_{1} bonds would project onto an effective S=1S=1 (for a full S=1S=1 projection, the total spin moment S⁡(S+1)=2S(S+1)=2 on a bond). Thus, we discover a simple but elegant property of the bluebellite Heisenberg Hamiltonian – it emerges as an effective S=1S=1 kagome system (see Fig. 1 (c)). This effective kagome lattice Hamiltonian will have two distinct first neighbor interactions for smaller triangles Jeff∝J2+J5J_{\rm eff}\propto J_{2}+J_{5}, and for slightly larger triangles Jeff′∝J3+J4J^{\prime}_{\rm eff}\propto J_{3}+J_{4}, leading to a breathing anisotropy (see Fig. 1 (b) and (e)) [51]. We have precisely evaluated the interactions in the effective S=1S=1 breathing kagome lattice by repeating the energy mapping with S=1/2S=1/2 moments connected by J1J_{1} bonds constrained to S=1S=1 (for details, see Ref. [41]). We find antiferromagnetic couplings Jeff=49​(2)J_{\rm eff}=49(2) K and Jeff′=18​(2)J^{\prime}_{\rm eff}=18(2) K, and the breathing anisotropy is Jeff/Jeff′≈2.7J_{\rm eff}/J^{\prime}_{\rm eff}\approx 2.7 (Fig. 1 (c)).

An analysis of the S=1S=1 breathing kagome AFM due to Ghosh et. al. revealed that the ground state of such a system is a trimerized singlet [52]. To understand this ground state one can start with isolated JeffJ_{\rm eff} triangles (see Fig. 1 (c)), i.e., set Jeff′J^{\prime}_{\rm eff} to zero. In this limit, the ground state is a product of pure singlets on each down triangle. When the Jeff′J^{\prime}_{\rm eff} is turned on, triplet fluctuations develop on this singlet, which for Jeff′≤JeffJ^{\prime}_{\rm eff}\leq J_{\rm eff} remain insufficient to conjure a phase transition, forming a stable trimerized singlet ground state for the system [52, 36, 53]. In the present case, a similar ‘trimerized’ state is also realized, which translates as a dimerized state. If one tunes J1→∞J_{1}\rightarrow\infty, this dimerized state on the maple-leaf lattice should continuously evolve to the trimerized singlet state of S=1S=1 breathing kagome. The trimerized state here is akin to the valence-bond solid state for the AFM spin-11 chain due to Affleck, Kennedy, Lieb and Tasaki [54]. In both cases, one sees the spin-11 as a combination of two spin-1/21/2, tries to satisfy the AFM interactions locally, and then projects a spin-11 out of two spin-1/21/2. Also note that for an AFM spin-11 chain with coupling equal to J2J_{2}, the spin-gap is 0.150.15 [55], which is slightly larger compared to the spin gap we obtain. A similar physics was seen for S=1S=1 kagome in Ref. [49].

Static and Dynamical Structure Factors.- We first calculate the static structure factor, S⁡(𝐪)=1N​∑i​jeı​𝐪⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​⟨𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j⟩S(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}e^{\imath\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}\langle\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}\rangle, using DMRG and bosonic theory. The DMRG result (Fig. 2 (a)), shows diffused peaks at the MM points of the fourth Brillouin zone (BZ). In contrast, the peaks from the low-energy bosonic theory (Fig. 2 (b)) are significantly shifted from the MM points. To understand this further, we exploit the relation between the kagome lattice and the maple-leaf lattice (see Fig. 1 (c)), to transform the static spin structure factor of kagome 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 order into the S𝐪S_{\mathbf{q}} for a maple-leaf system (see Ref. [41]) and find Bragg peaks at the MM points (see Fig. 2 (c)). We also introduce a relative spin canting across J1J_{1} bonds (see Fig. 2 (c)) and find it to be incapable of changing the Bragg peak positions. Therefore, a shift in the peaks in Fig. 2 (b) must have a quantum mechanical origin. To confirm this, we assume a state which is a product state of pure singlets on the J2J_{2} bonds. Note that this state is similar to the mean-field wavefunction for our bosonic theory. This state reproduces the shift in question (see Fig. 2 (d)). Thus, we infer that the shift in the maximum of S𝐪S_{\mathbf{q}} away from the MM points is due to the stabilization of the spin-singlets on the J2J_{2} bonds. The other modifications seen in Fig. 2 (b) are ascribed to triplet fluctuations.

It is apparent from Fig. 2 (b), that a shift in the peak results in an enlargement of the BZ of the S𝐪S_{\mathbf{q}}. A form factor calculation reveals that by traversing along either of the reciprocal vectors of the lattice, the structure factor is only periodic in seven reciprocal lattice spacing. Thus, the extended BZ of S𝐪S_{\mathbf{q}} is seven times larger than the actual BZ of the lattice (see Fig. 2 (e)). This significantly enhanced extended BZ is the reason behind the finite-size DMRG and bond-operator mean-field theory in the thermodynamic limit not agreeing in the calculation of S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}).

We further calculate the powder averaged static spin structure factor, S⁡(Q)=14​π​∫d​Ω𝐪^​S​(𝐪)S(Q)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\mathrm{d}\Omega_{\hat{\mathbf{q}}}S(\mathbf{q}), with Q=|𝐪|Q=|\mathbf{q}|, from both DMRG and the bond operator mean-field theory. We show the magnetic form factor, F⁡(Q)F(Q), modulated S⁡(Q)S(Q) in Fig. 3 (a). Apart from the static spin structure factor, we also calculate the dynamical spin structure factor, S⁡(𝐪,ω)=1N​∑i​jeı​𝐪⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​∫−∞∞d​t​eı​ω​t​⟨𝐒j​(t)⋅𝐒i​(0)⟩S(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}e^{\imath\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}te^{\imath\omega t}\langle\mathbf{S}_{j}(t)\cdot\mathbf{S}_{i}(0)\rangle, for this system using the bosonic mean-field theory. We use the extended BZ of the system and plot S⁡(𝐪,ω)S(\mathbf{q},\omega) along the high-symmetry lines in Fig. 3 (b).

Thermodynamic properties.- Capturing the finite temperature behavior precisely down to low temperature is a hard problem, but we can obtain qualitative information from our bond operator theory. We calculate specific heat using the bosonic mean-field theory (see [41]) and present it in Fig. 3 (c) together with the experimental result for the magnetic contribution to specific heat [2]. It shows a broad peak around 2222 K and matches the overall behavior of the experimental data. The specific heat shape that has been interpreted in terms of the Bonner-Fisher fit for the 1D Heisenberg chain [2] is captured well by our entangled 2D wavefunction. This may be rationalized by the fact [56] that zero-, one- and two-dimensional magnets can all have the same overall shape of specific heat, and magnetic susceptibility. The magnetic entropy calculation further validates effective spin-11 behavior of the system by approaching 12​ln⁡3\frac{1}{2}\ln{3} at high temperature (the factor of 1/21/2 is due to two spin-1/21/2 combining to form a spin 11), instead of ln⁡2\ln{2} which would be the case for a fully AFM system. The residual entropy comes from the interlocking of the spins across the J1J_{1} bonds at low temperature.

However, the sharp peak seen in the experiment at 1717 K, which was identified as the onset of a magnetic order [2], is not seen in our computation, and we find a magnetically disordered ground state instead. The appearance of a magnetic order is indicative of substantial structural changes in bluebellite at low temperatures. However, we believe that this anomalous behavior can also be attributed to the thermal activation of other excited states which live above the triplet excitations [41].

Conclusions.- We have determined the Heisenberg Hamiltonian for bluebellite by DFT energy mapping and found that two of the five couplings in the slightly distorted maple leaf lattice are ferromagnetic. Based on the DMRG result that the second largest antiferromagnetic exchange leads to very strong antiferromagnetic spin correlations, we have developed a bond operator mean field theory for bluebellite which gives us access to thermodynamic properties. Our calculated specific heat does not show a sharp ordering peak as the ground state for the Hamiltonian parameters determined for the room temperature crystal structure is magnetically disordered. However, there is excellent agreement in the overall shape of the specific heat, and we obtain the apparent Bonner-Fisher curve that was interpreted in terms of 1D physics [2] from our fully two-dimensional maple leaf Hamiltonian. Furthermore, focusing on a pattern of strong ferromagnetic spin correlations in both DMRG and bond operator theory, we find that bluebellite realizes an effective spin-1 breathing kagome lattice. We predict both static and dynamic spin structure factors and show how they can be understood based on the classically expected 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0} order of the effective kagome model. We would like to point out that the maple leaf Hamiltonian and the effective spin-1 kagome model are determined from a room temperature crystal structure; they are both expected to show a 1/3 magnetization plateau which was not observed in the T=4.2T=4.2 K magnetization process [2]. Therefore, it will be very interesting future work to determine a low temperature crystal structure of bluebellite experimentally and to study its Hamiltonian.

Supplemental Materials: Effective spin-1 breathing kagome Hamiltonian induced by the exchange hierarchy in the maple leaf mineral bluebellite

I Details of electronic structure calculations and energy mapping

The crystal structure of bluebellite Cu6​IO3​(OH)10​Cl\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{10}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{10}}\text{}}\text{Cl} has been determined from mineral samples [1] and from synthetic polycrystals [2]. In the latter case, hydrogen positions were not determined. As the magnetic measurements were performed for synthetic bluebellite, it is necessary to prepare the crystal structure for electronic structure calculations and energy mapping by adding and optimizing hydrogen positions. Furthermore, Cl, O2 and H2 all have coordinates (0,0,z), restricting their position by symmetry to an axis, and H2 needs to be placed between Cl and O2, in accordance with the Mills et al. structure [1]. At a distance dCl−O2=2.205d_{\rm Cl-O2}=2.205 Å, there is insufficient space for an O2-H2 bond and a Cl-H hydrogen bond. Therefore, Cl and O2 positions need to be optimized as well. For consistency, we optimize all O positions as well. The resulting structure is given in Table S1.

As explained in the main text, the large ferromagnetic J1J_{1} bonds of bluebellite lead to an effective spin-1 breathing kagome lattice behavior. In order to determine the exchange interactions of this effective model, we performed energy mapping in a 3×1×13\times 1\times 1 supercell with 18 Cu sites where we constrained moments adjacent to the J1J_{1} bond to be parallel. In this way, we determine the effective exchange interaction for the spin-1 breathing kagome lattice. As shown in Fig. S1, we perform the energy mapping for five different UU values. We use the same UU value that is relevant for the original maple leaf lattice (see main text, Fig. 1) to determine the effective Hamiltonian parameters. The result is Jeff=49​(2)J_{\rm eff}=49(2) K, Jeff′=18​(2)J^{\prime}_{\rm eff}=18(2) K, J1,eff⟂=−2​(3)J^{\perp}_{\rm 1,eff}=-2(3) K, J3,eff⟂=1​(2)J^{\perp}_{\rm 3,eff}=1(2) K, J2,eff=−3​(2)J_{\rm 2,eff}=-3(2) K, J2,eff′=1​(2)J^{\prime}_{\rm 2,eff}=1(2) K. Due to the error bars, not so much information about the subleading couplings can be obtained. It is clear that the effective kagome lattice has only very small interlayer couplings Ji,eff⟂J^{\perp}_{i,\rm eff}. The inplane second neighbor couplings on average appear to be slightly ferromagnetic.

II Details of bond-operator mean-field theory

Based on our findings from the DMRG calculations of the Hamiltonian for bluebellite, we now develop an effective low-energy bosonic theory for various reasons. First we want to obtain an better understanding of the system at the thermodynamic limit. Secondly, such an approximate theory allows us to calculate static and dynamic spin structure factor of the system very easily. Additionally, we can gain some insight of the thermodynamic properties of the system as well.

Upon carefully observing the NN spin-spin correlations obtained from DMRG (See Fig. 1 of main text), we propose that a minimal low-energy physics of the system can be well described by assuming that the ground state of the system is a dimerized singlet with strong singlet weights on the J2J_{2} bonds. To understand the effective low-energy physics of the system, we start with a J2−J3J_{2}-J_{3} hexagon as our unit cell, and only consider the three J2J_{2} bonds as our elementary block, \begin{gathered}\includegraphics[scale={0.14}]{./t1.pdf}\end{gathered}, described by the Hamiltonian

ℋ\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[scale={0.14}]{./t1.pdf}\end{gathered}} =\displaystyle= J2​∑b=1,2,3(S→2​b−1⋅S→2​b)\displaystyle J_{2}\sum_{b=1,2,3}\left(\vec{S}_{2b-1}\cdot\vec{S}_{2b}\right) (S3)
=\displaystyle= J2​(S→1⋅S→2+S→3⋅S→4+S→5⋅S→6),\displaystyle J_{2}\left(\vec{S}_{1}\cdot\vec{S}_{2}+\vec{S}_{3}\cdot\vec{S}_{4}+\vec{S}_{5}\cdot\vec{S}_{6}\right),

where b=1,2,3b=1,2,3 is the bond index (see Fig.S2). The ground state of this Hamiltonian is a product state of singlets forming on the 1​-​21\text{-}2, 3​-​43\text{-}4, and 5​-​65\text{-}6 spin pairs, which allows us to use the bond-operator formalism [3] to represent the spin operators as

S2​b−1α=−12(s^bt^bα†+s^b†t^bα)S_{2b-1}^{\alpha}=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{s}_{b}\hat{t}_{b}^{\alpha\dagger}+\hat{s}_{b}^{\dagger}\hat{t}_{b}^{\alpha}\right)\\ (S4a)
S2​bα=12(s^bt^bα†+s^b†t^bα).S_{2b}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\hat{s}_{b}\hat{t}_{b}^{\alpha\dagger}+\hat{s}_{b}^{\dagger}\hat{t}_{b}^{\alpha}\right). (S4b)

In writing the above representation, one makes use of the basis of the singlet, |sb⟩|s_{b}\rangle, and three triplets, |tb±1,0⟩|t^{\pm 1,0}_{b}\rangle, defined on the bond bb. On a Fock space with vaccum, |∅⟩b|\varnothing\rangle_{b}, the singlet and the triplet operators are defined as

|sb⟩=s^b†​|∅⟩b|s_{b}\rangle=\hat{s}_{b}^{\dagger}|\varnothing\rangle_{b} (S5a)
|tbm⟩=t^bm†|∅⟩b,|t^{m}_{b}\rangle=\hat{t}^{m\dagger}_{b}|\varnothing\rangle_{b}, (S5b)

with s^b\hat{s}_{b} and t^bm\hat{t}^{m}_{b} being bosonic operators. A boson number constraint

s^b†s^b+∑m=−1,0,1t^m†bt^mb=1\hat{s}_{b}^{\dagger}\hat{s}_{b}+\sum_{m=-1,0,1}\hat{t}^{m\dagger}_{b}\hat{t}^{m}_{b}=1 (S6)

must also be satisfied on every bond. In terms of the singlet and he triplet operators defined above ℋ\mathcal{H}_{\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[scale={0.14}]{./t1.pdf}\end{gathered}} reads as,

ℋ=−34J2∑bs^b†s^b+14J2∑b∑α=x,y,zt^α†bt^αb\mathcal{H}_{\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[scale={0.14}]{./t1.pdf}\end{gathered}}=-\frac{3}{4}J_{2}\sum_{b}\hat{s}_{b}^{\dagger}\hat{s}_{b}+\frac{1}{4}J_{2}\sum_{b}\sum_{\alpha=x,y,z}\hat{t}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b}\hat{t}^{\alpha}_{b} (S7)

where

t^x†=12(t^b−1†−t^b1†)\hat{t}^{x\dagger}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{t}^{-1\dagger}_{b}-\hat{t}^{1\dagger}_{b}\right) (S8a)
t^y†=i2(t^b−1†+t^b1†)\hat{t}^{y\dagger}=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{t}^{-1\dagger}_{b}+\hat{t}^{1\dagger}_{b}\right) (S8b)
t^z†=t^0†b.\hat{t}^{z\dagger}=\hat{t}^{0\dagger}_{b}. (S8c)

Next, we rewrite our full Hamiltonian and recast it in terms of the “coordinate” operator

Q^bα=12(t^iα†+t^iα)\hat{Q}_{b}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{t}_{i}^{\alpha\dagger}+\hat{t}_{i}^{\alpha}\right) (S9)

and its conjugate momentum operator

P^bα=i2(t^iα†−t^iα).\hat{P}_{b}^{\alpha}=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{t}_{i}^{\alpha\dagger}-\hat{t}_{i}^{\alpha}\right). (S10)

Thus, the final form of the full Hamiltonian, ℋ\mathcal{H}, on NucN_{\rm uc} unit-cells reads as,

ℋ≈ℋMF=e0Nuc+12∑𝐤∑α[λ𝐏^𝐤α†𝐏^𝐤α+𝐐^𝐤α†𝒱𝐤α𝐐^𝐤α].\mathcal{H}\approx\mathcal{H}_{\text{MF}}=e_{0}N_{\rm uc}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bf{k}}\sum_{\alpha}\left[\lambda\hat{\bf{P}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\hat{\bf{P}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha}+\hat{\bf{Q}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\mathcal{V}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha}\hat{\bf{Q}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha}\right]. (S11)

Here, e0=−3​J2​s¯2+34​J2+3​λ​s¯2−152​λe_{0}=-3J_{2}\overline{s}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}J_{2}+3\lambda\overline{s}^{2}-\frac{15}{2}\lambda, with s¯\overline{s} being the mean singlet amplitude on all the J2J_{2} bonds. λ\lambda is the Lagrange multiplier used to satisfy the boson number constraint in (S6) on average.

𝐏^𝐤α†=[P^1​𝐤α† P^2​𝐤α† P^3​𝐤α†]\displaystyle\hat{\bf{P}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}=\left[\hat{P}_{1\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\text{ }\hat{P}_{2\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\text{ }\hat{P}_{3\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\right] (S12)
𝐐^𝐤α†=[Q^1​𝐤α† Q^2​𝐤α† Q^3​𝐤α†]\displaystyle\hat{\bf{Q}}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}=\left[\hat{Q}_{1\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\text{ }\hat{Q}_{2\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\text{ }\hat{Q}_{3\bf{k}}^{\alpha\dagger}\right] (S13)

and

𝒱𝐤α=[λη12η31∗η12∗λη23η31η23∗λ]\mathcal{V}_{\bf{k}}^{\alpha}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda&\eta_{12}&\eta_{31}^{\ast}\\ \eta_{12}^{\ast}&\lambda&\eta_{23}\\ \eta_{31}&\eta_{23}^{\ast}&\lambda\end{bmatrix} (S14)

with

η12=s¯22​[−J3+(J5−J1)​ei​𝐤⋅𝐚𝟐+J4​ei​𝐤⋅𝐚𝟏]\eta_{12}=\frac{\overline{s}^{2}}{2}\left[-J_{3}+(J_{5}-J_{1})e^{i\bf{k}\cdot\bf{a}_{2}}+J_{4}e^{i\bf{k}\cdot\bf{a}_{1}}\right] (S15a)
η23=s¯22[−J3+(J5−J1)e−i𝐤⋅𝐚𝟏+J4e−i𝐤⋅(𝐚𝟏−𝐚𝟐)]\eta_{23}=\frac{\overline{s}^{2}}{2}\left[-J_{3}+(J_{5}-J_{1})e^{-i\bf{k}\cdot\bf{a}_{1}}+J_{4}e^{-i\bf{k}\cdot(\bf{a}_{1}-\bf{a}_{2}})\right] (S15b)
η31=s¯22[−J3+(J5−J1)ei​𝐤⋅(𝐚𝟏−𝐚𝟐)+J4e−i𝐤⋅𝐚𝟐].\eta_{31}=\frac{\overline{s}^{2}}{2}\left[-J_{3}+(J_{5}-J_{1})e^{i\bf{k}\cdot(\bf{a}_{1}-\bf{a}_{2})}+J_{4}e^{-i\bf{k}\cdot\bf{a}_{2}}\right]. (S15c)

Moreover, P^α†b​𝐤\hat{P}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b\bf{k}}’s and Q^α†b​𝐤\hat{Q}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b\bf{k}}’s are the Fourier components of P^bα†(𝐫)\hat{P}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b}(\bf{r})’s and Q^bα†(𝐫)\hat{Q}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b}(\bf{r})’s, respectively, i.e. P^b​𝐤α†=1/Nuc∑𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐫P^bα†(𝐫)\hat{P}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b\bf{k}}=1/\sqrt{N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\bf{k}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot{\mathbf{r}}}\hat{P}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b}(\bf{r}) and Q^b​𝐤α†=1/Nuc∑𝐤ei​𝐤⋅𝐫Q^bα†(𝐫)\hat{Q}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b\bf{k}}=1/\sqrt{N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\bf{k}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot{\mathbf{r}}}\hat{Q}^{\alpha\dagger}_{b}(\bf{r}).

ℋMF\mathcal{H}_{\text{MF}} now is a problem of three coupled differential equations, which one diagonalizes to obtain

ℋMF=e0Nuc+∑m∑𝐤∑αω𝐤,mα(γ𝐤,mα†γ𝐤,mα+12)\mathcal{H}_{\text{MF}}=e_{0}N_{\rm uc}+\sum_{m}\sum_{\bf{k}}\sum_{\alpha}\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\left(\gamma_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha\dagger}\gamma_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}+\frac{1}{2}\right) (S16)

where γ𝐤,mα\gamma_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha} are renormalized triplon operators, and

ω𝐤,mα=λ⁡(λ−12​s¯2​ξ𝐤,mα)\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}=\sqrt{\lambda\left(\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\overline{s}^{2}\xi_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)} (S17)

with

ξ𝐤,mα=2​−p𝐤3​cos⁡[13​cos−1⁡(3​q𝐤2​p𝐤​−3p𝐤−2​π3​m)]\xi_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}=2\sqrt{-\frac{p_{\mathbf{k}}}{3}}\cos\left[\frac{1}{3}\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3q_{\mathbf{k}}}{2p_{\mathbf{k}}}\sqrt{-\frac{3}{p_{\mathbf{k}}}}-\frac{2\pi}{3}m\right)\right] (S18)

and

p𝐤\displaystyle p_{\mathbf{k}} =\displaystyle= −(|η12|2+|η23|2+|η31|2)\displaystyle-\left(|\eta_{12}|^{2}+|\eta_{23}|^{2}+|\eta_{31}|^{2}\right) (S19)
q𝐤\displaystyle q_{\mathbf{k}} =\displaystyle= 2​Re​(η12​η23​η31).\displaystyle 2\text{Re}\left(\eta_{12}\eta_{23}\eta_{31}\right). (S20)

The ground state of the system is given by the vaccum of the quasi-particles, γ𝐤,mα\gamma_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}, i.e., the ground state energy per site of the system is given by,

eg=e06+112​Nuc​∑m∑𝐤∑αω𝐤,mαe_{g}=\frac{e_{0}}{6}+\frac{1}{12N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\bf{k}}\sum_{\alpha}\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha} (S21)

The unknown mean-field parameters, λ\lambda and s¯2\overline{s}^{2} are determined by minimizing ege_{g}, which leads to the following self-consistent equations

λ=J2+112​Nuc​∑m∑𝐤∑αλ​ξ𝐤,mα2​ω𝐤,mα\lambda=J_{2}+\frac{1}{12N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\bf{k}}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\lambda\xi_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}}{2\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}} (S22a)
s¯2=52−112​Nuc​∑m∑𝐤∑α4​λ−s¯2​ξ𝐤,mα2​ω𝐤,mα.\overline{s}^{2}=\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{12N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{m}\sum_{\bf{k}}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{4\lambda-\overline{s}^{2}\xi_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}}{2\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}}. (S22b)

To access the finite temperature properties from the bond-operator mean-field theory we employ the methodology used by Normand et. al. [4]. First of all, a thermal occupation function of hard–core bosons is impossible. This problem can be tackled by imposing the local hard-core constraint (S6) at the global level to obtain effective statistics as,

n⁡(ω𝐤,mα,β)=exp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα)1+∑m,𝐤,αexp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα),n(\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha},\beta)=\frac{\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}{1+\sum_{m,\bf{k},\alpha}\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}, (S23)

where β\beta is the inverse temperature. The magnetic specific heat, hereafter, is easily derived by taking a second derivative of the free-energy with respect to temperature. The magnetic specific heat thus obtained reads as,

Cmag​(β)=∑m,𝐤,α[(β​ω𝐤,mα)2​exp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα)1+∑m,𝐤,αexp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα)−{β​ω𝐤,mα​exp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα)1+∑m,𝐤,αexp⁡(−β​ω𝐤,mα)}2].C_{\text{mag}}(\beta)=\sum_{m,\bf{k},\alpha}\left[\frac{\left(\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)^{2}\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}{1+\sum_{m,\bf{k},\alpha}\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}-\left\{\frac{\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}{1+\sum_{m,\bf{k},\alpha}\exp\left(-\beta\omega_{\mathbf{k},m}^{\alpha}\right)}\right\}^{2}\right]. (S24)

The results obtained from the finite temperature calculations are depicted in Fig. 3 of the main text.

III Further results from DMRG

The ground state energy of the bluebellite Hamiltonian, introduced in the main text, is calculated via DMRG using the ITENSOR [5] package. For the calculations, we use three different sized spin tubes with N=2N=2, 33, and 44 unit cells along the circumference of the tube. Along the length of the tube we always take 2​N2N unit cells. Thus we do our calculations on L=48,108,192L=48,108,192 site clusters. For L=48L=48 and 108108, we perform 3030 sweeps with a maximum bond dimension 20482048. For L=192L=192 the number of sweeps was reduced to 2424. The ground state energy obtained via these calculations are shown in Fig. S3 (a). We perform a linear fitting of the energies to obtain a finite size scaling. The spin-spin correlations from two central sites are shown in Fig. S3 (b). A fast decay of the long range spin-spin correlations is apparent there. Next, to access the thermodynamic properties of the system, we calculate the magnetic specific heat by using,

Cmag∝1L​T2​[⟨H^2⟩−⟨H^⟩2]C_{\text{mag}}\propto\frac{1}{LT^{2}}\left[\langle\hat{H}^{2}\rangle-\langle\hat{H}\rangle^{2}\right] (S25)

where, TT is the temperature of the system and ⟨Q^⟩\langle\hat{Q}\rangle is the thermal average of an observable Q^\hat{Q}. For this part of the calculation we choose the 4848 site cluster. We perform 2424 sweeps with a maximum bond dimension of 512512 and calculate 480480 exited states. We estimate that for a LL site cluster there will be L/2L/2 strong singlets forming on the J2J_{2} bonds. Each such singlet would have 33 excited triplet states. Therefore, we need more than 3​L/23L/2 excited states to capture the finite temperature physics which will be missed by the bond-operator calculations. Thus it is an extremely costly calculation and also prone to numerical errors, and thus we only perform it on a small cluster to get an idea of the thermodynamic properties of the system which we show in Fig. S3 (c). We see an anomalous behavior occurring at ∼10​ K\sim 10\text{ K} which becomes exceedingly pronounced with increasing number of excited states considered. We believe this comes from the thermal activation of the excited states that live above the triplets. We believe the anomalous behavior seen in the experiments at 1717 K is also related to that.

IV Luttinger-Tisza analysis of the bluebellite

The full model Hamiltonian of bluebellite is not amenable to a solution in the classical, i.e. S→∞S\to\infty limit, where spin operators are replaced by vector spins. Therefore, we resort to the Luttinger-Tisza approximation [6, 7], where the normalization of the spins is enforced only on average, allowing for analytical solution of the model. The corresponding band-structure in Fig. S4 shows a flat lowest band with a band-with of 4% of J~\tilde{J}, and an almost degenerate area around the Γ\Gamma point, featuring soft minima along the Γ\Gamma–MM direction. While in the classical limit, even in the Luttinger-Tisza approximation, this energy landscape implies an ordered ground state, quantum fluctuations can access these low-lying states by allowing for variations in the spin expectation values. Therefore, the flatness of the lowest Luttinger-Tisza band indicates the probability for the quantum model to avoid long-range order, as we find for bluebellite.

V Further information for static and dynamical structure factors

V.1 Maple-leaf structure factor as a basis expanded kagome structure factor

In the main text we have mentioned that the bluebellite Hamiltonian behaves as an effective spin-11 kagome system with a breathing anisotropy. Here, we demonstrate under such an assumption how one can calculate the static structure factor for the maple-leaf system from the same for a kagome system. The static structure factor for a non-Bravais system like kagome is given by,

S⁡(𝐪)=1N​∑i​j∑k​k′ei​𝐪⋅(R→i−R→j)​ei​𝐪⋅(b→k−b→k′)​⟨S→k′​(R→j)⋅S→k​(R→i)⟩,S(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\sum_{kk^{\prime}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\vec{R}_{i}-\vec{R}_{j})}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\vec{b}_{k}-\vec{b}_{k^{\prime}})}\langle\vec{S}_{k^{\prime}}(\vec{R}_{j})\cdot\vec{S}_{k}(\vec{R}_{i})\rangle, (S26)

where R→i\vec{R}_{i} are the positions of the unit-cells, and b→k\vec{b}_{k} are the basis vectors. Next, to go to the maple-leaf unit cell from the kagome unit-cell one needs to expand each basis site of kagome into two sites. For the kk-th basis site of kagome, this is achieved by creating two sites at b→k±δ→k\vec{b}_{k}\pm\vec{\delta}_{k} (the δ→k\vec{\delta}_{k}’s are given in Fig. S5). Thereafter, the static structure factor for maple-leaf lattice is derived from the spin-spin correlations calculated for the effective kagome system reads as,

S⁡(𝐪)=1N​∑i​j∑k​k′ei​𝐪⋅(R→i−R→j)​ei​𝐪⋅(b→k−b→k′)​ei​𝐪⋅(±δ→k∓δ→k′)​⟨S→k′​(R→j)⋅S→k​(R→i)⟩.S(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{ij}\sum_{kk^{\prime}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\vec{R}_{i}-\vec{R}_{j})}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\vec{b}_{k}-\vec{b}_{k^{\prime}})}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\pm\vec{\delta}_{k}\mp\vec{\delta}_{k^{\prime}})}\langle\vec{S}_{k^{\prime}}(\vec{R}_{j})\cdot\vec{S}_{k}(\vec{R}_{i})\rangle. (S27)

This has been used to produce Fig. 2 (c) in the main text, for which we start with an effective breathing kagome system with spins replaced by classical vectors. For this system the ground state is known to be degenerate with both 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 and 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} coplanar orders. For a 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} order, the high intensity occurs at the KK points of the extended Brillouin zone (BZ), while for 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 order, it occurs at the MM points of the extended BZ.

V.2 Extended Brillioun zone

The form factor, f𝐆f_{\mathbf{G}}, for a maple-leaf system is given by

f𝐆∝∑jexp⁡(i​𝐆⋅𝐯j)f_{\mathbf{G}}\propto\sum_{j}\exp(i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{j}) (S28)

where 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j} are the six basis vectors of the lattice, G=ν1​𝐛1+ν2​𝐛2G=\nu_{1}\mathbf{b}_{1}+\nu_{2}\mathbf{b}_{2} is a site on the reciprocal lattice defined by the reciprocal vectors 𝐛1\mathbf{b}_{1} and 𝐛2\mathbf{b}_{2} (ν1\nu_{1} and ν2\nu_{2} are integers). The maxima of |f𝐆|2|f_{\mathbf{G}}|^{2} occur for all combinations of ν1\nu_{1} and ν2\nu_{2} such that mod(ν1+2​ν2,7)=0\mod(\nu_{1}+2\nu_{2},7)=0, i.e., by traversing along 𝐛1\mathbf{b}_{1} or 𝐛2\mathbf{b}_{2} the structure factor is only periodic in seven reciprocal lattice spacings. Therefore, the extended BZ of the structure factor is seven times bigger than the actual BZ of the lattice (see Fig. 2 (e) in the main text).

V.3 Magnetic form factor for Cu2+

In Fig. 3 (a) of the main text, we show the magnetic form factor |F⁡(Q)|2|F(Q)|^{2} modulated S⁡(Q)S(Q), where we use

F⁡(Q)=\displaystyle F(Q)= 0.0232​e−34.969​(Q4​π)2+0.4023​e−11.564​(Q4​π)2\displaystyle 0.0232e^{-34.969\left(\frac{Q}{4\pi}\right)^{2}}+0.4023e^{-11.564\left(\frac{Q}{4\pi}\right)^{2}} (S29)
+\displaystyle+ 0.5882​e−3.843​(Q4​π)2−0.0137\displaystyle 0.5882e^{-3.843\left(\frac{Q}{4\pi}\right)^{2}}-0.0137

for Cu2+ ions [8].
